items.title: [news.climate.columbia.edu] Study finds human-caused warming reversed early North American glaciation
items.content_html:
🌾 🔧 ✏️

A study published in Science says the Barnes Ice Cap on Canada’s Baffin Island, the last remnant of the Laurentide Ice Sheet, began expanding about 2,000 years ago. Researchers identify that growth as the start of a new glacial period. The ice began retreating around 1960 as summer warming caused it to lose more ice than it gained. The team reconstructed the ice cap’s history using vegetation preserved beneath the ice and dates from exposed rocks. The researchers define the start of a glacial period as the resumption of ice-sheet growth, differing from models that place the next glaciation thousands or tens of thousands of years in the future. Models cited by the researchers project that the Barnes Ice Cap could disappear within the next few centuries. The researchers say rising atmospheric carbon dioxide makes a return to glacial conditions extremely unlikely.

items.title: [The Guardian Global Development] Have scientists finally found a way to save the banana from disaster?
items.content_html:
With the climate crisis and diseases threatening one of the world’s most popular fruits, researchers are hoping a breakthrough in breeding techniques could give the Cavendish banana a certain future

Love them or loathe them, bananas are one of the world’s most popular fruit. But a combination of the climate crisis and new killer diseases have had growers concerned over the banana’s threatened extinction, something that would impose a huge toll on farmers in countries from Guatemala to Malawi, alongside eradicating a staple food.

Now researchers say they have made fresh advances in the race to save them from disaster. This month, Yelloway – a research collaboration between Chiquita, the world’s largest banana company, and the crop-improvement company KeyGene – announced it had developed a fully fertile Cavendish banana, meaning it may be possible, through cross-breeding, to create new banana varieties that are commercially viable and resistant to disease.

items.title: [scitechdaily.com] Stanford team revives bleached corals through brief clone contact
items.content_html:
🎨 🌾 🔧 🪶 🌲 🏔️ 🔭 ✏️

Stanford researchers report that bleached coral fragments fully recovered within seven weeks in laboratory tests after brief contact with healthy, genetically identical clones, according to a study published Oct. 14 in *Science Advances*. Contact lasting five days to a week was sometimes enough; bleached fragments kept a few millimeters away from healthy partners died. Microscopic channels in the corals’ tissues aligned, allowing beneficial algae to move between fragments within three days. Inside bleached fragments, algae populations doubled every four days during the second week. The method requires matching clones, limiting its use across reefs. The researchers plan to test other ways to deliver algae, including collecting it from healthy corals before heat waves.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] Scientists finally uncover why statins can cause muscle pain
items.content_html:
🎨 🏔️ ✏️

Scientists have uncovered a surprising reason why statins, the widely prescribed cholesterol-lowering drugs that help prevent heart attacks and strokes, can sometimes cause muscle pain, weakness, and even severe muscle damage. Using advanced imaging technology, researchers discovered that statins can attach to a crucial protein in muscle cells and force open a channel that normally controls calcium flow. This causes calcium to leak continuously, potentially damaging muscle tissue.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] Just 3,000 steps a day may help slow Alzheimer's, scientists find
items.content_html:
🎨 🌾 🔧 🪶 🌲 🏔️ 🔭 ✏️

Walking just 3,000 steps a day could help slow Alzheimer’s-related brain changes, according to new research. Scientists discovered that physical activity was linked to less buildup of harmful tau proteins and nearly half the cognitive and functional decline, even in people already showing early signs of the disease. The strongest benefits appeared at 5,000 to 7,500 daily steps, suggesting that the popular 10,000-step goal may not be necessary.
